messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samir was twelve when the plaster cracked down the hallway, but it was his father’s voice that carved itself into him first. The man who once taught him to throw a baseball became a stranger who shouted, slammed doors, and dragged a chair across the floor until the wood splintered. When Samir tried to piece together those years, he found himself staring at hyper-detailed snapshots in his mind—the exact scuff marks on the baseboard, the way the streetlamp caught the dust in the air—while the hours before and after remained completely erased. He knew that if he forced himself to deliberately recall the sequence of events, the images would simply dissolve, leaving only a heavy, hollow pressure in his chest. As an adult, that wiring followed him to the framing floor. The moment a city inspector’s cruiser pulled into the gravel lot or a project manager raised his voice over the concrete mixer, Samir’s breath would catch and his shoulders would lock against his ribs, the physical readiness for violence kicking in before his mind could even process the request. When those authority figures approached with sudden expectations, they did not just bring physical alarm; they unlocked the exact, hyper-detailed snapshots of the hallway nights, while leaving the surrounding hours completely dark. Samir had come to believe that his body was the first to sound the alert, so he quickly learned to sidestep any discussion about deadlines, assuming that when projects dragged on longer than expected, disaster was already loading in the wings. Those sudden intrusions of memory did not just haunt him; they dictated his next moves. When a photograph of a shattered doorframe would surface without warning, Samir would immediately scan the crew for tight jaws or shifting stances, convinced that violence was only a breath away. He would retreat into a mental fog, replaying old clips of how he used to be before the violence took hold, because dwelling on a safer past felt less dangerous than facing the present. And because the memories kept surfacing unbidden, he began to interpret any future planning as a trap, flinching whenever anyone asked him to commit to a schedule months out. What frightened him most was that the past kept bleeding into the present, turning every neutral timeline into a countdown. On the scaffolding, the constant scanning of faces and the dread of delayed permits turned his body into a warning system. When a forklift backed up slower than expected, the physical tension in his chest would surge, and the only thing that stopped him from shouting or fleeing was the habit of slipping into a private fantasy where he was no longer on a job site. The physical alarm pulled sharper, unbidden images of the splintered chair and cracked plaster to the front of his mind, making the event feel like it was happening now rather than years ago. He would retreat into those daydreams, and the act of escaping only hardened the boundaries around his trauma; the longer he drifted away, the more impossible it became to pull the actual footage of the event from his mind, leaving only the raw snapshots intact. Over the years, the habit of avoidance and the refuge of internal daydreams did exactly what he feared they would. By refusing to engage in disagreements and retreating into his own head, he slowly rewired his environment; every time he avoided a discussion, the unresolved tension festered until even a neutral question from a coworker triggered the same old alarm. His refusal to engage meant that even minor requests from supervisors now landed like personal attacks, and the distance he built into his own head only kept his nervous system permanently dialed up. He stopped looking forward to anything, convinced that planning only painted a target on his back. Samir, now forty-one, finally walked into a clinic after a routine inspection triggered a full-body tremor that lasted nearly an hour, leaving him unable to climb back onto the framing line. He had come to believe that his body was betraying him, that the constant scanning and the mental escapes were failing him, and that the only way to keep his job—and his life—intact was to finally sit down with someone who understood how fear works. He hoped, more than anything, to learn how to stand in a room without his heart racing, and to figure out why the future kept feeling like a threat.
